title: A study exploring the relationship between social media use and nutrition-related practices among secondary school students in London (Sutton, El Zein & Maragkoudaki, Proceedings of the Nutrition Society 85(OCE1): E38, 2026)
screen_reason: Mixed-methods questionnaire study of 24 London adolescents. It reports a share of respondents who say they have encountered nutrition misinformation on social media (71% of 24), which meets the RECALL criterion. The published item is a conference abstract, so only this one share with its denominator is available.

estimates.platform: social media (TikTok most used, 68%); no platform split for the misinformation item
estimates.date: not reported (Nutrition Society Winter Conference, 20-21 January 2026)
estimates.measure_type: % of adolescent respondents who reported having encountered nutrition misinformation on social media
estimates.denominator: 24 London adolescents aged 16-18+ (54% female) recruited from three secondary schools/colleges across London
estimates.definition: Respondent reported having encountered nutrition misinformation on social media (questionnaire item; wording and reference window not reported in the abstract)
estimates.misinfo_def: no definition given; the abstract refers to "widespread nutrition misinformation on these platforms" and "online nutrition misinformation"
estimates.source_quote: Although 71% had encountered nutrition misinformation, few consistently verified the nutrition qualifications of creators (13%), and most didn't routinely fact-check (54%).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent self-report in a questionnaire analysed in SPSS; no definition of misinformation supplied to participants and no external verification
estimates.moderator_quote: A mixed-methods study design was used with a sample of London adolescents (n=24, aged 16-18+) recruited from three secondary schools/colleges across London. Questionnaires and four focus groups were used for data collection.
estimates.notes: Very small convenience sample (n=24); 71% corresponds to 17/24 (70.8%). The published item is a conference abstract, so no methods detail (item wording, recall window, sampling procedure, response rate) is available; breadth coded 'false' because the paper uses the bare term 'misinformation' with no gloss. Year is the conference/publication year; no fieldwork date is reported.

missed_or_uncertain: Other percentages in the abstract are not misinformation measures: 61% used social media as primary nutrition information source, 68% TikTok, 57% fitness influencers, 13% verified creator qualifications, 54% did not routinely fact-check, 79% altered their diet, 71% purchased nutrition products, 71% influenced by brands/influencers, 90% of males reported positive feelings. None of these is a share of misinformation encountered, shared or classified.

rob.design: Mixed-methods (questionnaire + four focus groups) with a convenience sample of 24 students aged 16-18+ from three London secondary schools/colleges; recruitment via the 'Nourish to Flourish' project; no response rate, no item wording, no coding procedure and no reliability statistics reported (conference abstract).
rob.item6_quote: Although 71% had encountered nutrition misinformation, few consistently verified the nutrition qualifications of creators (13%), and most didn't routinely fact-check (54%).
rob.item10_quote: Of the 24 participants (54% female), a majority (61%) used SM as their primary source for nutrition information, with TikTok (68%) and fitness influencers (57%) being the most popular platform and account type, respectively.
